The study in one paragraph

In the Q4 Pulse 3 survey, adults recruited through Prolific who had used an AI chatbot for a health question in the past 6 months copied and pasted one recent health conversation from their chat history into the survey, then answered questions about it: who it was about, their goal, whether the goal was met, how they felt before and after, and what they did next. After removing 1 off-topic paste, 59 participants were analysed. 7 pastes held only the AI’s text, which leaves 52 chats with at least one message written by the participant. These 52 chats are the base for every percentage below unless stated otherwise. Most people used ChatGPT, and most chats were about the participant’s own health.

How we coded the chats

1. Split each pasted chat into the participant’s messages and the AI’s replies, and remove personal names.

2. Codebook: write each label with a plain definition, what is in and out, and rules for close calls. Pilot it, and have the analyst approve and lock (“freeze”) it.

3. Code: 3 independent AI coders applied the frozen codebook without seeing earlier labels. The label at least 2 of 3 agreed on was kept, and every evidence quote was checked word for word against the chat.

4. Review: the analyst (the researcher) reviewed every flag and close call and made the final decisions.

Agreement: the 3 coders agreed almost perfectly (kappa 0.97 to 1.00). Kappa shows that the coders were consistent, not that they were right, which is why the analyst reviewed close calls.

Results at a glance

  • What people asked first. The most common opening requests were general facts about health (15 of 52 chats) and “why is this happening to me?” (14).
  • Short questions, long answers. Participants’ messages had a median of 15 words; the AI’s replies had a median of 277.5 words, about 16 times longer.
  • Most chats were short. 20 of 52 chats (38%) stopped after the first message.
  • Background was rarely volunteered. Background information (age, health history, medicines and so on) came with the first message or after the AI asked. Nobody added it later on their own.
  • Preliminary: goals were usually met. 40 of 52 (77%) said yes, and 8 said partly.
  • Preliminary: the AI suggested medicines in 12 chats (23%) and named a brand in 8. In every chat where it suggested a medicine, it also said to see a doctor or other professional.

2. How long the messages were

Figure 2. Words in each participant message compared with the AI reply that followed (140 pairs). Hover over a box to see a message of about the typical length.
Takeaway: The AI’s reply was longer than the message it answered 95% of the time, typically about 16 times longer.
Figure 3. Number of participant messages per chat (59 participants). Hover over a bar to see a first message from a chat of that length.
Takeaway: Most people sent only one or two messages; long back-and-forth chats were rare.

3. How the conversations unfolded

We followed each chat through three moments: what the person opened with, what their 2nd message did, and when they shared background information about themselves. The next two figures show the same 52 chats in two ways: a flow chart and a decision tree. Table 2 explains the background-timing labels used in both.

Table 2. What the background-timing labels mean. A fourth label, “on their own later” (shared without being asked), was in the codebook but no chat used it, so it is not shown in the charts.

TermWhat it means
Background informationFacts that give the AI context about the person: age, weight or height, health history and other conditions, medicines, how long the problem has lasted, other symptoms beyond the main problem, habits or activity level, and recent events or care that led up to the problem. It does NOT include the main complaint itself, more description of the main problem, or "what if" symptoms.
With the first messageBackground information was already in the first message.
After the AI askedThey shared background information after the AI asked a question, or invited it (for example "If you tell me X, I can...").
Never sharedThey never shared any background information in the chat.
Figure 4. Opening request, then the 2nd message, then when background information was shared (52 chats). Percent of all 52 chats; band thickness shows the number of chats. Background timing is shown only for chats whose 2nd message shared more or asked what to do. Hover over a dark bar or a coloured band.
Takeaway: Half the chats opened by asking to understand, 38% stopped after one message, and the most common next step was sharing more about themselves.
Figure 5. The same 52 chats drawn as a decision tree. Each opening group has its own branches; percent of all 52 chats. Hover over any box.
Takeaway: Whatever people opened with, the most common outcome was stopping after one message or sharing more about themselves.

4. Preliminary: what people wanted from the chat, and whether they got it

PRELIMINARY. These results come from draft codebooks that have not yet been piloted or independently coded. Numbers may change.
Figure 6. Main goal, from each person’s own survey answer (52 chats). Hover over a bar to see example survey answers.
Takeaway: The most common goal was to find out what might be wrong (20 chats), followed by finding out what to do and learning about a condition, medicine or test.
Figure 7. Was the goal met? By opening request group. Hover over a bar segment to see an example answer.
Takeaway: 77% said their goal was met; 6 people said it was met but they were also told to see a doctor. The groups are small, so differences between them are not reliable.

5. Preliminary: how direct was the AI’s advice?

PRELIMINARY. These results come from draft codebooks that have not yet been piloted or independently coded. Numbers may change.
Figure 8. Advice ladder: percent of the 52 chats in which the AI reached each step. Steps go from general information up to giving a dose. Hover over a step to see an example AI reply.
Takeaway: Most AI advice stayed at general information or self-care tips; the AI suggested a type of medicine or a specific medicine in 23% of chats and gave a dose in 2.
Figure 9. Advice compared with safety messages, by the highest step reached. Hover over a bar to see an example of the safety message.
Takeaway: The more direct the advice, the more often the AI also said to see a doctor and gave a warning; every chat with a medicine suggestion included a see-a-doctor message.
Figure 10. Medicines the AI suggested, by number of chats, coloured by whether a brand name was used. Supplements and vaccines are shown as tags; they are not counted on the advice ladder. Hover over a row to see where the AI mentioned it.
Takeaway: Ibuprofen (7 chats) and acetaminophen (6) were suggested most, usually with a brand such as Advil or Tylenol; most other medicines appeared in a single chat.

Limitations

  • Small sample. With 52 chats, one chat is about 2 percentage points, and the confidence ranges are wide. Differences between subgroups should be treated as hints, not findings.
  • Self-selected online sample. Participants were recruited on Prolific and chose which conversation to share, so they may not represent all people who use AI for health.
  • Pasted chats. People copied the chats themselves; some pastes may be incomplete or edited, and 7 held only the AI’s text.
  • AI coders. The coders were independent runs of an AI model. High agreement shows consistency, not accuracy; the analyst reviewed close calls.
  • Preliminary sections. Goals, goal met and the advice ladder (sections 4 and 5) come from draft codebooks that are not yet piloted or independently coded.
  • Hover examples. Each example is one short, de-identified excerpt chosen to illustrate a category. It is not a summary of every chat in that category.

Questions you could explore with these data

These questions use the survey answers listed in the appendix. Some could also be linked to the chat results shown above.

  • Did feelings change from before to after the chat (the PANAS items), and by how much?
  • How often did people say an AI had named a medication (med_mentioned), and how did they say the AI talked about it (med_framing, med_alternatives)?
  • How strongly did people feel the AI recommended action (action_ai_rec), and what did they do afterwards (action_taken open answers)?
  • Do the chatbot used (detail_chatbot), the type of health topic (detail_topic) or who the chat was about (convo_about) relate to how strongly action was recommended?
  • Does prior knowledge of the condition (detail_prior_knowledge) or how long they had it (detail_duration) relate to feelings before and after the chat?
  • What goals did people describe (convo_goal_oe), and did they feel the goal was met (convo_goal_met_oe)?
  • Do any of these answers differ by age, gender, race and ethnicity, urban or rural living, or insurance?
